courses.title: Programming Fundamentals
courses.description: Become fluent with code, execution, debugging, and clean input handling.

courses.title: Course 00: Engineering Judgment And Sage Learning Operating System
courses.description: Complete Course 00: Engineering Judgment And Sage Learning Operating System with inspectable artifacts, realistic failure repair, proof evidence, explain-back, transfer, and portfolio packaging.

concepts.title: Your First Program
concepts.question: How do I write and run my first program?
concepts.summary: Write and run your very first program: make the computer print an exact line of text on screen, and understand the edit → run → see-output loop that every programmer lives in.

concepts.title: Variables: Names for Values
concepts.question: What is a variable in programming and how do I use one?
concepts.summary: Store a value in a named variable, change it by reassigning, and use a variable in a calculation — so your programs can remember and reuse values instead of repeating them.

concepts.title: Numbers & Strings: The Everyday Types
concepts.question: What is the difference between numbers and strings in Python?
concepts.summary: Tell numbers and text apart, do arithmetic on numbers, convert between text and numbers when you need to, and build a clean formatted line by dropping values into text with an f-string.

concepts.title: Reading Input: Make the Program Listen
concepts.question: How do I read user input in Python and convert it to a number?
concepts.summary: Make your program RECEIVE data instead of only using values you typed in: read a line with input(), convert it to a number with int() when you need to do math, and print an exact line built from what you read.

concepts.title: Booleans & Decisions: Make the Program Choose
concepts.question: How do if, elif, and else statements make a program choose?
concepts.summary: Make your program CHOOSE: compare values to get a True/False answer, combine conditions with and/or/not, and run different code with if / elif / else so the program reacts instead of always doing the same thing.

concepts.title: Lists: Hold Many Values at Once
concepts.question: How do I store many values in a Python list?
concepts.summary: Hold many values under one name with a list: create one, read an item by its position, measure it with len(), add to it with append(), and ask whether something is in it.

concepts.title: Loops: Do Something for Every Item
concepts.question: How do for loops and range() work in Python?
concepts.summary: Do something to every item in a sequence without copy-paste: loop over a list with for, repeat an action a fixed number of times with range(), and build up a result (a total or a count) in a variable as you go.

concepts.title: Functions: Name and Reuse a Block of Code
concepts.question: How do I define a function in Python with def and return?
concepts.summary: Define your own function with def, give it inputs (parameters), send a value back with return, and call it to reuse a block of code — so you stop copy-pasting the same steps and start naming them.

concepts.title: Build & Ship a Tiny Program
concepts.question: How do I combine variables, loops, and functions into a complete program?
concepts.summary: Combine everything from First Steps — a variable, a list, a loop, an if, and a function — into ONE small program that processes real in-code data and prints a useful result. This is your first genuinely shipped program.

concepts.title: Input Validation: Trust Nothing at the Boundary
concepts.question: How do I validate untrusted input at the boundary?
concepts.summary: Write a validator that rejects malformed, wrong-type, out-of-range, and hostile input at the boundary — and explain what belongs at the client, server, and database.

concepts.title: Error Handling: Make Failures Loud, Safe, and Diagnosable
concepts.question: How should I handle exceptions without swallowing errors?
concepts.summary: Handle errors so failures surface loudly, users get a safe clear message, operators get enough context to diagnose — and you never swallow an exception.

concepts.title: Functions & Modules: Build Small, Testable Units
concepts.question: What is a pure function and why is it easier to test?
concepts.summary: Write a small, single-purpose, PURE function with a clear signature — and a test that proves it — then refactor a side-effecting function to be testable.

concepts.title: Types & Data: Know What a Value Really Is
concepts.question: Why does a value's type matter and how do I convert types safely?
concepts.summary: Identify a value's type, convert input safely at the boundary, choose the right data structure, and write a function that can't be fooled by a string that looks like a number.

concepts.title: Control Flow: Guard Clauses & Clean Loops
concepts.question: What are guard clauses and how do they replace nested if statements?
concepts.summary: Flatten nested conditionals with guard clauses, write a correct loop, and avoid the classic loop bugs (off-by-one, infinite loop, mutate-while-iterating).

concepts.title: Files & I/O: Read Safely, Close Always
concepts.question: How do I read a file safely in Python with a context manager?
concepts.summary: Read a file with a context manager so it always closes, parse it into a dict, stream large files instead of loading them, and handle the missing-file case explicitly.

concepts.title: Testing & Debugging: Catch the Bug Before Prod
concepts.question: How do I write a test that actually catches a real bug?
concepts.summary: Write the cheapest test that catches a real bug — including the edge/negative case the happy path misses — and turn a bug into a regression test.

concepts.title: CLI Safety: Safe Defaults & Dry Runs
concepts.question: How do I build a CLI tool with safe defaults and a dry-run mode?
concepts.summary: Build a command that defaults to dry-run, never defaults to production, and requires explicit confirmation for high-blast-radius actions.

concepts.title: Git Fundamentals: Atomic Commits You Can Trust
concepts.question: What is an atomic Git commit and why does it matter?
concepts.summary: Make small atomic commits with clear messages, use branches to isolate work, and recover safely when something goes wrong — never panic-force-push a shared branch.

concepts.title: The Problem Frame
concepts.question: How do I frame an ambiguous engineering problem before jumping to solutions?
concepts.summary: Take one ambiguous, real decision you are facing (or a realistic one) and write the Frame: the actual problem in one sentence, the non-negotiable constraint, the decision to be made, and the specific failure you fear — solution-free.
concepts.courseTitle: Course 00: Engineering Judgment And Sage Learning Operating System

concepts.title: The Diagnostic Route
concepts.question: How do I rank hypotheses and design tests to diagnose a failure?
concepts.summary: Take the feared failure from your Frame and write the Diagnostic Route: at least three ranked hypotheses for the cause, the single test that would DISQUALIFY each, and the order you would run them — cheapest disqualifier first.
concepts.courseTitle: Course 00: Engineering Judgment And Sage Learning Operating System

concepts.title: The System Map
concepts.question: How do I map a system to find the blast radius of a failure?
concepts.summary: Draw the smallest accurate map of the system your decision lives in — components, directed flow, the suspect edge — then name the blast radius if that edge fails.
concepts.courseTitle: Course 00: Engineering Judgment And Sage Learning Operating System

concepts.title: The Retrieval Protocol
concepts.question: How do I practice engineering decisions from memory with calibrated confidence?
concepts.summary: Turn the three moves of this module — Frame, Route, Map — into a closed-note Retrieval Protocol you can run from memory on a real decision, logging a calibrated confidence (1–5) on each step and catching where confidence outran reality.
concepts.courseTitle: Course 00: Engineering Judgment And Sage Learning Operating System

concepts.title: Tiny Artifact: Make the Decision Inspectable
concepts.question: What is a decision memo and how do I make an engineering decision inspectable?
concepts.summary: Turn an ambiguous engineering decision into one small, named, inspectable artifact — engineering_judgment_decision_memo.md — that a reviewer can open and judge in under two minutes.
concepts.courseTitle: Course 00: Engineering Judgment And Sage Learning Operating System

concepts.title: Failure Injection: Break Your Own Decision First
concepts.question: How do I stress-test my own engineering decision by injecting failure?
concepts.summary: Deliberately inject a realistic failure into the decision from your engineering_judgment_decision_memo.md, and add a failure autopsy that names what breaks, how you would detect it, and what you would do — turning a happy-path memo into one that survives reality.
concepts.courseTitle: Course 00: Engineering Judgment And Sage Learning Operating System

concepts.title: Tradeoff Decision: Defend the Call Under Pressure
concepts.question: How do I document and defend an engineering tradeoff decision?
concepts.summary: Turn the decision in your engineering_judgment_decision_memo.md into a defended tradeoff: a comparison of real options against the constraints that actually bind, with a chosen option, a reversal condition, and the risk if you are wrong.
concepts.courseTitle: Course 00: Engineering Judgment And Sage Learning Operating System

concepts.title: Testa Proof: Prove It With the Strongest Evidence
concepts.question: What is the strongest evidence to prove an engineering decision holds?
concepts.summary: md with a Testa proof: the strongest available evidence that the decision actually holds — executable test, contract/schema check, a domain check (a11y/security/reliability/eval), or a reviewer rubric when execution is impossible — and a one-line portfolio claim that names the proof, not the topic.
concepts.courseTitle: Course 00: Engineering Judgment And Sage Learning Operating System

concepts.title: Explain It Back: The Feynman Gate
concepts.question: How do I use the Feynman technique to prove I understand a technical decision?
concepts.summary: Prove you actually understand a hard decision by teaching it back in a fixed order — problem, context, artifact, failure, proof, tradeoff, repair, transfer — by name, pointing at the exact evidence a reviewer would inspect.
concepts.courseTitle: Course 00: Engineering Judgment And Sage Learning Operating System

concepts.title: The Review Rubric: Score Your Own Work
concepts.question: How do I build a rubric to score my own engineering work?
concepts.summary: Build a review rubric: a fixed, inspectable scoring contract that turns "this feels solid" into a defensible number. Then score your own decision memo with it — honestly, respecting the caps — so a second reviewer applying the same rubric lands within a point of you.
concepts.courseTitle: Course 00: Engineering Judgment And Sage Learning Operating System

concepts.title: The Repair Loop: Fix the Weakest Part
concepts.question: How do I systematically fix the weakest part of my work and prove it improved?
concepts.summary: Run the repair loop: take the single weakest part your rubric flagged, fix exactly that, re-apply the same rubric, and prove the score moved for the right reason. The output is a repair log that shows pre-score, root cause, the smallest fix that lifts the cap, and the re-tested post-score.
concepts.courseTitle: Course 00: Engineering Judgment And Sage Learning Operating System

concepts.title: The Spacing Queue: Make It Stick
concepts.question: How does spaced repetition keep engineering judgment from decaying?
concepts.summary: Build a spacing queue that keeps your hard-won judgment from decaying: each card is a decision you recall without notes at expanding intervals, interleaved across topics, with calibrated confidence routing shaky-but-confident recalls back into repair.
concepts.courseTitle: Course 00: Engineering Judgment And Sage Learning Operating System

concepts.title: Transfer Challenge
concepts.question: How do I transfer an engineering decision method to an unfamiliar domain?
concepts.summary: Apply the engineering-judgment pattern — decide, show the artifact, name the failure, prove it, defend it — COLD to a domain you were never taught. Produce a decision memo that survives a reviewer who never saw your original work.
concepts.courseTitle: Course 00: Engineering Judgment And Sage Learning Operating System

concepts.title: Package Evidence
concepts.question: How do I package evidence so a reviewer can verify my engineering judgment?
concepts.summary: Turn last lesson's decision into packaged EVIDENCE — a ledgered, inspectable trail that lets a reviewer who was not in the room verify your judgment without taking your word for it. The portfolio claim must name the proof, not the topic.
concepts.courseTitle: Course 00: Engineering Judgment And Sage Learning Operating System

concepts.title: Unlock Gate
concepts.question: What is an honest gate and how do I know when my work actually passes?
concepts.summary: Run an honest unlock gate on your own work: it opens ONLY when the evidence exists, refuses to round a gap up to a pass, and routes every miss to a specific repair before re-checking. Gate yourself the way a reviewer would — and pass or repair honestly.
concepts.courseTitle: Course 00: Engineering Judgment And Sage Learning Operating System

concepts.title: Capstone Rehearsal
concepts.question: How do I assemble a mastery packet that proves engineering judgment end to end?
concepts.summary: Rehearse the whole course as one gate. Assemble a mastery packet that proves every capability Course 00 built — decide under ambiguity, package evidence, gate honestly, transfer judgment — and defend it the way you would in a real review. Pass it for real and you have earned what comes next.
concepts.courseTitle: Course 00: Engineering Judgment And Sage Learning Operating System
